lines: The model's own offline score looked genuinely strong, and production lift sat at exactly nothing.
One feature, orders over the last month, was computed from the table's current state rather than from the click's own moment.
So a training row from months ago ended up counting orders that hadn't even happened yet at the time of that click.
An offline score that strong, with nothing to show for it online, is genuinely a sign the training data itself lied.
How would you have caught this before launch, and what single join rule actually prevents it?
answer: More rows joined the exact same wrong way just repeat the identical leak at a larger scale, never close it.
The real fix joins every feature as it was actually known at the event's own moment, never anything later than that.

lines: One feature definition compiles two separate ways: a batch computation over history, and an incremental one for serving.
That single definition is genuinely what closes the gap where training and serving computed the same feature two different ways.
A feature computed one way for training and another for serving trains a model on something it will never actually see live.
Each feature's own freshness need decides which path it actually takes.
A feature updated once daily sits comfortably on batch; one needed fresh every event genuinely needs the stream.
The same logic runs on both paths, on purpose, so neither computation quietly drifts away from the other over time.
Building a training row for a past event means joining each feature exactly as it was known back then, never later.
A join that instead grabs today's latest value reaches straight into the future the model is actually being asked to predict.
The same planted feature, joined two different ways against one dataset, scored against a held-out future neither join had seen.
The join that reached ahead scored far better than its honest counterpart, and that gap is exactly the leak, now measured.
A sampled check keeps comparing the online store's value for an entity against what the offline computation says it should be.
That comparison runs as a standing service-level objective with its own alert, because skew arrives silently, never with a warning first.
A changed upstream column or a different rule for missing values is genuinely enough to quietly pull the two stores apart.
Turning on a brand-new feature only from today leaves every past training row with nothing in that column at all.
A proper backfill reconstructs each one of those point-in-time values from raw history, validated in shadow before anyone trusts it live.

Notice what actually closed the gap between a strong offline score and a flat production lift: one feature definition feeding both stores, a join landing on the event's own moment instead of today, and a parity check that never stops running.
The feature count here grows by a full order of magnitude.
Every single join still lands correctly, exactly as it did before, because its correctness never depended on how many other features exist.
So what's actually the next bottleneck?
answer: A bigger join isn't actually what breaks, since each feature's own join depends only on that one feature and that one event.
What stops being affordable is checking every feature's parity at the same rate; the sampling and alert volume are the real bottleneck.
